topic: Physics — Waves in air, fluids and solids: Transverse and longitudinal waves
subject: combined-science

items.q: Which statement about the types of wave is correct?
items.correct: A wave may be either transverse or longitudinal.
items.misconception: Every wave is transverse, as the diagrams show.
items.why: The word 'wave' is bound to a picture of a wavy curve from primary school onwards, and that picture is a transverse one. The wavy curve is only one type. Sound in air is longitudinal, with compressions and rarefactions instead of crests and troughs.
items.random_wrong: The type depends on how the wave gets drawn.

items.q: Ripples on a water surface are an example of a transverse wave. Why?
items.correct: The water surface oscillates up and down, across the direction the ripple moves.
items.misconception: The water surface oscillates back and forth along the direction the ripple travels.
items.why: The two words are learned as a pair without being tied to their meanings, so students remember that there is a contrast but not which label goes with which motion. Link the word to its meaning: 'longitudinal' shares its root with 'along', so the oscillation is along the direction of travel; 'transverse' shares its root with 'across'.
items.random_wrong: The water is carried forwards across the pond as every ripple passes it.

items.q: A sound wave travels through air. What is a rarefaction in this wave?
items.correct: A region where the air particles are further apart.
items.misconception: A region where the air particles are pushed together.
items.why: Particle diagrams show rarefactions as noticeably emptier bands, and the two long words are easily swapped when they are learned as a pair. The particles are only spread out, never removed. A rarefaction is a region of lower pressure that still contains air; a compression is the opposite, where the air is squashed together.
items.random_wrong: A region where the air particles move across the wave.

items.q: Which statement about a sound wave travelling through air is correct?
items.correct: It is longitudinal, with compressions and rarefactions.
items.misconception: It is transverse, because it is displayed as a wavy trace.
items.why: Oscilloscope traces and the waveforms shown by recording software are drawn as curves, and students read the shape of the graph as the shape of the wave. The curve is a graph of pressure or displacement against time, not a picture of the air. The air itself is pushed together and pulled apart along the direction of travel.
items.random_wrong: It is longitudinal, so it must have a solid to travel through.

items.q: What is the difference between a longitudinal wave and a transverse wave?
items.correct: In a longitudinal wave the oscillations are parallel to the direction of travel, and in a transverse wave they are perpendicular to it.
items.misconception: A longitudinal wave carries the material of the medium along with it, while a transverse wave carries only the energy.
items.why: Everyday transport moves the stuff as well as the effect, so students assume that delivering energy means delivering matter. Each particle passes the disturbance on to its neighbour and returns to its own position, so energy arrives while the medium stays where it was.
items.random_wrong: In a longitudinal wave the oscillations are perpendicular to the direction of travel, and in a transverse wave they are parallel.

items.q: One end of a long slinky is pushed and pulled repeatedly along its length. Which description of the wave produced is correct?
items.correct: Longitudinal, because the coils vibrate along the direction the wave travels.
items.misconception: Transverse, because the coils vibrate across the direction that the wave travels.
items.why: The two words are learned as a pair without being tied to their meanings, so students remember that there is a contrast but not which label goes with which motion. Link the word to its meaning: 'longitudinal' shares its root with 'along', so the oscillation is along the direction of travel; 'transverse' shares its root with 'across'.
items.random_wrong: Longitudinal, because the coils are carried along to the far end of it.

items.q: A ball floats on a still pond while ripples pass beneath it. Which observation is evidence that the water itself does not travel?
items.correct: The ball bobs up and down but stays in the same place.
items.misconception: The ball is carried away to the far bank by ripples.
items.why: Ripples look like humps of water sliding across the surface, and in everyday speech a 'wave' at the seaside really is water rushing up a beach. A floating ball bobs up and down in the same place as ripple after ripple passes under it. It is not carried to the far bank, so only the wave crosses the pond.
items.random_wrong: The ball edges a little further forwards as each ripple passes.

items.q: A loudspeaker plays loud music. Which observation is evidence that the air itself does not travel across the room to the listener?
items.correct: No draught is felt by the listener as the music plays.
items.misconception: A steady breeze can be felt coming from the loudspeaker cone.
items.why: Students know sound needs air, and a moving speaker cone does push on the air, so they picture a puff of air travelling all the way to the listener. No draught is felt from a loudspeaker playing music, and a candle flame in front of it is not blown out. The air near the cone simply oscillates and passes the disturbance on.
items.random_wrong: A candle flame placed in front of the loudspeaker is blown out.

items.q: What decides whether a wave is transverse or longitudinal?
items.correct: The direction of the oscillations compared with the direction in which the wave travels.
items.misconception: It depends on how the wave is drawn: a curvy line means transverse and a row of lines means longitudinal.
items.why: Each type is met through one standard diagram, so the diagram style becomes the definition rather than an illustration of it. The same wave can be represented in several ways. Ask what the particles of the medium are doing, not what the picture looks like.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Can a longitudinal wave travel through air?
items.correct: Yes. Sound waves travelling through air are longitudinal.
items.misconception: Longitudinal waves need a solid such as a slinky, so a wave travelling through air must be transverse.
items.why: Longitudinal waves are usually demonstrated on a slinky, so students attach the wave type to the springy solid used in the demonstration. Any material that can be compressed can carry a longitudinal wave. Air is squeezed and stretched by a loudspeaker exactly as the slinky is by a hand.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does a floating object drift forwards as ripples pass beneath it?
items.correct: No. It bobs up and down about the same position while the ripples move on.
items.misconception: Each passing ripple nudges the float a little further forwards, so it slowly drifts to the far side.
items.why: Floats on a real pond do drift because of wind and currents, and students credit the ripples with the movement they can see. In still water the float returns to the same place after every ripple. Any drift is caused by wind or a current, not by the wave itself.
